title: The Blue Cab
question: 15% of cabs are Blue; a witness (80% accurate) says the hit-and-run cab was Blue. Most people answer 80%. What is the actual chance?
correctExplanation: About 41% — Bayes: (0.15×0.8) / (0.15×0.8 + 0.85×0.2) ≈ 0.41. Base rates drag testimony down hard.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is about 41%, blending both. Neither witness-alone (80%) nor base-alone (15%): Bayes weights accuracy by priors. Green cabs' sheer numbers swamp honest mistakes.
lessonContent:
Priors drag testimony down hard.
Bayes weights accuracy by base rates.
Sheer numbers swamp honest mistakes.
Neither witness nor base decides alone.
Share this: blend one testimony tonight.

title: The Split Verdict
question: A disease hits 1% of people; a test is 99% accurate both ways. You test positive with no symptoms. What is the chance you are ill?
correctExplanation: Roughly half of positives — true positives (1%×99%) roughly equal false positives (99%×1%). Rarity splits positives evenly.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is roughly half of positives. Accuracy misleads at low priors: healthy multitudes each roll 1% false-positive dice, matching the sick few one-for-one. Screen positives need retests, not panic.
lessonContent:
Rarity splits positives evenly often.
Healthy multitudes roll dice too.
Accuracy misleads at low priors.
Retest positives; never panic first.
Share this: halve one test scare.

title: The Flagged Flyer
question: One in a million travelers means harm; a scanner false-alarms on 1% of innocents. Flags pour in daily. What dominates the flagged lists?
correctExplanation: Mostly false alarms — 10,000 innocents per million each roll 1%: ~100 false flags per real one. Rare targets drown in common errors.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is mostly false alarms. Threats, misses, and profits miss it: base arithmetic buries the scanner. Screening rare targets manufactures innocent majorities.
lessonContent:
Rare targets drown in common errors.
Base arithmetic buries good scanners.
Innocent majorities fill flagged lists.
Screening rarity manufactures falsehood.

title: The Meadow Error
question: An expert testified two cot deaths in one family meant murder (1-in-73-million by squaring single risk). Mothers were jailed, later freed. What was abused?
correctExplanation: False independence — squaring assumes independence; shared genes and environments correlate risks hugely. Meadow's arithmetic jailed the innocent.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is false independence. Equipment, juries, and wood miss it: risks within families correlate, so multiplication fabricates astronomical odds. Dependence ignored becomes injustice squared.
lessonContent:
Correlations forbid naive squaring.
Independence assumed jails innocents.
Family risks correlate hugely always.
Dependence ignored squares injustice.
Share this: unmultiply one scary number.

title: The Hiring Screen
question: 90% of applicants can't do the job; a screening test is 80% accurate. Most candidates who pass will actually do what?
correctExplanation: Fail despite passing — unqualified multitudes swamp qualified few even at 80% accuracy. Pass lists mirror applicant pools, not test quality.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is fail despite passing. Brilliance, lawsuits, and refusals miss it: 90% base times 20% error beats 10% base times 80% hits. Screens inherit their pools.
lessonContent:
Pass lists mirror applicant pools.
Unqualified multitudes swamp good tests.
Screens inherit pools, never transcend.
Base-heavy hiring needs base-aware reading.
Share this: read one pass list skeptically.

title: The Spam Folder
question: 99% of your mail is legitimate; your filter is 95% accurate. What fills the spam folder most?
correctExplanation: Legitimate mail — 1% of the vast legit majority outnumbers 95% of tiny spam. Filters starve on base rates too.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is legitimate mail. Princes, empties, and viruses miss it: 99%×5% false alarms beat 1%×95% catches. Ham floods filters built for spam.
lessonContent:
Ham floods spam-built filters reliably.
Majorities mistyped outnumber minorities caught.
Filters starve on base rates too.
Accuracy misleads at skewed priors.

title: The Truthful Crowd
question: With very few liars among thousands screened, even accurate lie detectors mostly flag whom?
correctExplanation: Truthful people — rare liars hide among flagged innocents: base rates convict the honest. Detector positives prove little alone.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is truthful people. Criminals, inventors, and puppies miss it: thousands of honest each roll small false-positive dice. Screening rarity frames the innocent.
lessonContent:
Rarity frames innocents routinely.
Honest thousands roll error dice.
Positives prove little at low priors.
Detectors accuse majorities wrongly.
Share this: acquit one flagged innocent.

title: The Thin Signal
question: Stellar job interviews barely budge hiring odds beyond résumé base rates — yet managers overweight them hugely. What should interviewers remember?
correctExplanation: Weak signals — unstructured interviews add drops of validity atop base rates. Charm misleads; files decide.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is weak signals. Charm, handshakes, and suits miss it: Meehl showed thin cues barely move priors. Overweighting interviews wastes base-rate wisdom.
lessonContent:
Thin cues barely move priors.
Charm misleads; files decide hiring.
Overweighting wastes base wisdom.
Interviews add drops, never floods.
Share this: discount one stellar interview.

title: The Formula Edge
question: What consistently outperforms expert intuition at predicting parole outcomes, illness courses, and job success?
correctExplanation: Statistical formulas — actuarial tables beat clinicians by applying base rates mechanically. Formulas don't flinch, tire, or charm.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is statistical formulas. Crystals, guts, and chats miss it: Meehl's century of contests crowns tables over experts. Base rates mechanized outperform intuitions romanticized.
lessonContent:
Tables beat experts mechanizing bases.
Formulas never flinch or charm.
Contests crown actuarial methods yearly.
Romantic intuitions lose reliably.

title: The Calm Forecaster
question: A pundit achieves 95% 'recession forecast' accuracy. Investigation shows one simple habit. What is it?
correctExplanation: Never predicting one — recessions are rare, so perpetual calm scores ~95%. Accuracy without discrimination is empty.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is never predicting one. Tips, models, and bribes miss it: always-calm forecasts ride base rates to fake accuracy. Discrimination, not hit rate, measures forecasters.
lessonContent:
Perpetual calm rides base rates.
Fake accuracy needs no skill.
Discrimination measures forecasters truly.
Hit rates lie without base context.

title: The Home Stretch
question: Most car crashes happen within miles of home. Does this mean home roads are uniquely dangerous?
correctExplanation: No — exposure volume: most miles happen near home, so most crashes do too. Denominators drive counts, not danger.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no, exposure volume explains it. Driveways, neighbors, and avoidance miss it: familiar roads host familiar mileage. Counts follow miles, never menace.
lessonContent:
Counts follow miles, never menace.
Denominators drive crash tallies.
Familiar roads host familiar mileage.
Exposure explains home-heavy stats.

title: The Survivor Memoir
question: Dropout-billionaire memoirs inspire students to quit school. What do the memoirs systematically hide?
correctExplanation: The failed majority — survivors write; the ruined stay silent. Memoirs sample winners, hiding base rates of ruin.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the failed majority. Ghosts, menus, and paper miss it: survivorship filters stories before binding. Winner shelves hide loser warehouses.
lessonContent:
Winner shelves hide loser warehouses.
Survivors write; ruined stay silent.
Memoirs sample success exclusively.
Base rates bury myths reliably.
Share this: shelve one dropout fantasy.

title: The Name Gap
question: Identical résumés with different names drew sharply different callback rates in a famous field experiment. What did the gap reveal?
correctExplanation: Systematic gaps — Bertrand and Mullainathan: names moved callbacks with qualifications fixed. Discrimination measured cleanly.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is systematic gaps. Fonts, paper, and providers miss it: identical merits, different responses. Field experiments isolate bias beautifully.
lessonContent:
Identical merits, different responses.
Field experiments isolate bias cleanly.
Names move callbacks measurably.
Patterned gaps demand structural fixes.

title: The Vague Prophet
question: Vague earthquake forecasts ('a big one soon, somewhere') seem to hit often. What makes them look accurate?
correctExplanation: Wide nets — big windows plus vague places guarantee hits by chance. Precision would expose emptiness.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is wide nets. Expertise, luck, and honesty miss it: broad predictions can't miss. Narrow the window and prophets go quiet.
lessonContent:
Broad predictions cannot miss ever.
Precision would expose emptiness fast.
Vagueness guarantees false accuracy.
Narrow windows silence prophets.

title: The Fitting Reading
question: Psychic readings feel accurate because they fit nearly everyone who hears them. What are such statements?
correctExplanation: Barnum statements — vague generalities feel personal to all. Flattery plus probability poses as paranormal.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is Barnum statements. Peers, labs, and theorems miss it: 'you have untapped potential' fits billions. Generality impersonates insight.
lessonContent:
Generality impersonates insight reliably.
Vague flattery fits billions at once.
Personal feeling proves nothing general.
Barnum feeds on self-recognition.

title: The Closest Face
question: Witnesses pick the lineup face closest to memory even when the culprit is absent. What goes wrong?
correctExplanation: Relative judgment — witnesses choose best-available instead of answering absent. Lineups without the culprit still produce picks.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is relative judgment. Perfection, photography, and sketches miss it: comparative choosing replaces absolute recognition. Best-of-six is not identification.
lessonContent:
Best-of-six is never identification.
Comparative choosing replaces recognition.
Absent culprits still yield picks.
Absolute judgments need blank options.

title: The Narrow Band
question: SAT scores predict weakly within elite colleges though strongly across all schools. What shrinks the campus link?
correctExplanation: Range restriction — admitted bands vary little, so correlations starve. Narrowed samples hide real relationships.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is range restriction. Leaks, cheating, and fonts miss it: elite ranges truncate variance that powers prediction. Selected samples mute true links.
lessonContent:
Truncated variance starves correlations.
Selected samples mute true links.
Narrow bands hide real relationships.
Range rules prediction strength.
Share this: un-narrow one sample.

title: The Zebra Surge
question: After one famous rare-disease case airs, doctors over-diagnose it for months. What inflates the rare diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vivid precedents — availability hijacks differential diagnosis: recent zebras outshout common horses. Memory availability prescribes.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is vivid precedents. Textbooks, scopes, and coffee miss it: one televised zebra reweights every hoofbeat. Recency prescribes disproportionately.
lessonContent:
Recency prescribes disproportionately.
Televised zebras reweight hoofbeats.
Availability hijacks differentials daily.
Memory vividness misleads clinics.
Share this: hear hooves, think horses.

title: The Vanished Fund
question: Published fund returns look stellar partly because dead funds vanish from the records. What hides?
correctExplanation: Dead funds — survivorship edits history: closed losers exit averages, leaving winners. Records remember victors only.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is dead funds. Winners, taxes, and birthdays miss it: liquidated losers leave the database, inflating survivors. Averages of the living lie about the born.
lessonContent:
Databases forget the liquidated.
Survivors inflate historical averages.
Records remember victors exclusively.
Living averages lie about births.

title: The Cluster Scare
question: Most neighborhood cancer clusters turn out to be chance groupings in small populations. What explains them?
correctExplanation: Random clustering — small numbers clump naturally: Texas-sharpshooter maps draw bullseyes around bullets. Chance paints targets.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is random clustering. Conspiracies, fluoride, and towers miss it: Poisson clumps in tiny samples routinely. Drawn bullseyes follow bullets, never predict them.
lessonContent:
Small numbers clump naturally always.
Bullseyes follow bullets, never lead.
Chance paints alarming targets.
Poisson explains most scares fully.

title: The Sober Count
question: Sober drivers dominate accident tallies year after year. Does this indict sobriety as dangerous?
correctExplanation: Road majorities — sober miles dominate roads, so sober crashes dominate counts. Majorities populate every tally.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is road majorities. Bans, drunkenness, and fraud miss it: base populations fill numerators. Counts follow exposure, never vice.
lessonContent:
Base populations fill all numerators.
Majorities populate every tally taken.
Counts follow exposure, never vice.
Numerators need denominators always.

title: The Gilded Lab
question: Nobel Prizes cluster in a handful of labs far beyond chance expectation. What concentrates them?
correctExplanation: Cumulative advantage — prestige attracts talent and funds, which attract prizes, which attract more. Matthew effects compound in science.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is cumulative advantage. Coffee, campuses, and janitors miss it: resources beget results beget resources. Rich labs get richer systematically.
lessonContent:
Resources beget results beget resources.
Prestige compounds systematically always.
Matthew effects govern gilded labs.
Rich get richer measurably here.

title: The Spontaneous Cure
question: Desperate patients trying sugar pills sometimes recover dramatically. What explains most 'miracle cures' without real treatment?
correctExplanation: Spontaneous remission — bodies heal unassisted on schedules no treatment owns. Regression plus biology explains miracles.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is spontaneous remission. Quanta, magic, and charisma miss it: natural histories include recoveries that treatments then claim. Baselines heal without billing.
lessonContent:
Baselines heal without any billing.
Natural histories include recoveries.
Regression plus biology explains miracles.
Treatments claim ambient healing often.

title: The Prior Habit
question: What single habit most reliably defeats base-rate neglect in everyday reasoning?
correctExplanation: Prior-checking — asking 'how common is this anyway?' before updating on evidence. Priors first, testimony second.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is prior-checking. Volume, speed, and caffeine miss it: background rates anchor every inference. Habits beat brilliance in debiasing.
lessonContent:
Background rates anchor inferences.
Priors first, testimony second always.
Habits beat brilliance in debiasing.
Ask commonness before updating.

title: The Sick Prescription
question: Aggressive treatments correlate with worse outcomes. Before condemning the drugs, what must be checked?
correctExplanation: Confounded prescriptions — sicker patients get stronger drugs: indication confounds outcome. Severity prescribes, then kills.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is confounded prescriptions. Colors, salaries, and music miss it: confounding by indication inverts apparent effects. The ill receive most and fare worst — unsurprisingly.
lessonContent:
Severity prescribes, then kills, spuriously.
Indication confounds outcome readings.
Sickest receive strongest drugs first.
Confounders invert apparent effects.
